figures.name: Clement of Alexandria
figures.places: Studied under teachers in Greece, southern Italy, Syria and Palestine; settled in Alexandria, Egypt, as a pupil and then successor of Pantaenus; left Egypt around the persecution of 202; later found with Bishop Alexander in Cappadocia and Jerusalem.
figures.role: Christian teacher and presbyter of Alexandria; head of the catechetical teaching there after Pantaenus; teacher of Origen (Eusebius, Church History 6.6).
figures.status_note: Honoured as a saint in the Coptic tradition and commemorated on Anglican calendars (Episcopal Church, 5 December). Once listed in Western martyrologies on 4 December, he was dropped when the Roman Martyrology was revised under Pope Clement VIII, and Benedict XIV upheld this in 1748 because his life was little known, he never had a public cult, and some of his teachings were thought suspect (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1908). The sixth-century Gelasian Decree lists "the works of the other Clement, of Alexandria" among books not received. No council condemned him. Cautions for a reader: when he says "the Gnostic" he means the mature Christian who truly knows God, not the heretical Gnostics he fought; he held a partly Stoic ideal of freedom from passions, and he could say Christ ate only so that people would not think Him a phantom (Stromata 6.9). The ANF left Stromata Book 3 (on marriage and sex) in Latin.
figures.hook: He wanted Christians to read Plato without fear, called the whole of life a festival, and told the story of the old apostle John chasing a bandit chief up a mountain to bring him home.

stories.story: He hunted for teachers across the Greek world: one in Greece, one in southern Italy, others in the East, one in Assyria, one a Hebrew in Palestine. Only when he tracked down the last, hidden in Egypt, did he "find rest". He calls that teacher (Pantaenus, per Eusebius) "the true, the Sicilian bee", gathering from the meadow of prophets and apostles.

He retold, as "not a tale but a narrative", how the aged apostle John entrusted a young convert to a bishop. The youth drifted into a gang and became its bloodiest captain. John rode alone to the bandits' mountain, chased the fleeing captain, and cried, "Why, my son, do you flee from me, your father, unarmed, old?" The man wept, was "baptized a second time with tears", and John did not leave until he had restored him to the Church. Clement tells it to prove that true repentance is never too late.
stories.source: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? 42

stories.story: Around 211 Bishop Alexander, then a confessor in prison, sent a letter to the church at Antioch by Clement's hand and called him "the blessed presbyter, a man virtuous and approved", who "has strengthened and built up the Church of the Lord". In a later letter to Origen, Alexander named "the holy Clement, my master and benefactor". Historians infer that Clement had left Alexandria during the persecution of 202; Eusebius himself does not say he fled.

He wrote a practical rule book for ordinary Christian life, The Instructor, that goes down to beds, beards, hair dye, shoes, table manners and how loudly to laugh. It ends with a hymn to Christ, one of the oldest Christian hymns whose author we know.
stories.source: The Instructor, Books 2 and 3; the Hymn to Christ the Saviour at the end of Book 3

stories.story: Eusebius says Origen studied under him as a boy in Alexandria.

temperament.evidence: His ideal Christian is "at once grave and cheerful in all things": grave because turned towards God, cheerful because of the good things God has given.
He refuses to follow one school: "whatever has been well said by each of those sects ... this eclectic whole I call philosophy."

temperament.trait: Writes in a deliberately scattered way
temperament.evidence: He says his Miscellanies are not a neat garden but "like an umbrageous and shaggy hill", mixing fruit trees and barren ones on purpose, to hide the fruit from thieves.

temperament.trait: A fussy moralist about daily manners
temperament.evidence: He sets rules for smiling, drinking without "contortions of the face", sleeping on hard beds so as to be "easily awaked", and never plucking the beard.

temperament.trait: Gentle towards the rich, severe towards their flatterers
temperament.evidence: He opens his sermon on wealth by calling those who praise the rich "flatterers and base" and "godless and treacherous", then spends it reassuring rich believers that they can be saved.
temperament.source: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? 1-3

genuine_lines.quote: the Word of God became man, that you may learn from man how man may become God.
genuine_lines.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Holding festival, then, in our whole life, persuaded that God is altogether on every side present, we cultivate our fields, praising; we sail the sea, hymning; in all the rest of our conversation we conduct ourselves according to rule.
genuine_lines.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: It is then, as appears, the greatest of all lessons to know one's self. For if one knows himself, he will know God; and knowing God, he will be made like God, not by wearing gold or long robes, but by well-doing, and by requiring as few things as possible.
genuine_lines.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Some men, in truth, live that they may eat, as the irrational creatures, whose life is their belly, and nothing else. But the Instructor enjoins us to eat that we may live.
genuine_lines.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: The way of truth is therefore one. But into it, as into a perennial river, streams flow from all sides.
genuine_lines.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For man is not to laugh on all occasions because he is a laughing animal, any more than the horse neighs on all occasions because he is a neighing animal.
genuine_lines.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: But the multitude are frightened at the Hellenic philosophy, as children are at masks, being afraid lest it lead them astray.
genuine_lines.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: His whole life is prayer and converse with God.
genuine_lines.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent

misattributed.line: The "Letter to Theodore" quoting a "Secret Gospel of Mark", often cited online as Clement's.
misattributed.truth: Known only from an 18th-century handwritten copy that Morton Smith reported finding at the Mar Saba monastery in 1958; the manuscript is no longer available for examination. Scholars remain divided on whether it is genuine Clement or a modern forgery. Do not use it as Clement's voice.

misattributed.line: "Clement taught that Christians should give away all their wealth."
misattributed.truth: The reverse. His sermon Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? argues that Jesus told the rich young man to strip his soul of passions, not to throw away property (sections 11-15).

misattributed.line: "It is the greatest of all lessons to know one's self; for if one knows himself, he will know God" is sometimes flagged online as a fake or as Socrates.
misattributed.truth: It is genuine Clement: The Instructor 3.1 (ANF). He builds on the Delphic "know yourself" but the sentence is his.

opinions.position: A Christian may keep wealth. Money is a tool, neither good nor bad; what must go are greed and the passions. Jesus's command to sell everything is about the soul, not the bank balance.
opinions.side_note: Keep and use wealth well (against giving it all away).
opinions.quote: So let no man destroy wealth, rather than the passions of the soul, which are incompatible with the better use of wealth. So that, becoming virtuous and good, he may be able to make a good use of these riches.
opinions.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most churchgoing Christians today live this way and would agree; radical voices (some Catholic Workers, Anabaptists, Tolstoyans, many young idealists) would side with the rich young man reading and sell everything. Among the Fathers it is contested: Clement is the classic moderate against Basil, Chrysostom and the monks. A good split statement.

opinions.topic: new: giving to people who may not deserve it
opinions.position: Do not try to sort the poor into deserving and undeserving. You will guess wrong, and it is better to help some who do not deserve it than to miss one who does.
opinions.side_note: Give to all who ask, without screening.
opinions.quote: Do not you judge who is worthy or who is unworthy. For it is possible you may be mistaken in your opinion. As in the uncertainty of ignorance it is better to do good to the undeserving for the sake of the deserving, than by guarding against those that are less good to fail to meet in with the good.
opinions.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly split. Many people today insist on giving only through vetted charities, or not giving cash to beggars; others say give freely and let God judge. Excellent quiz material.

opinions.position: No one is past repentance. A person who lived badly for years can, after turning back, outweigh all of it; the story of John and the bandit proves that even a baptized man who became a killer can be restored.
opinions.side_note: For second chances, even after grave sins committed after baptism.
opinions.quote: it is possible for the man who formerly led a bad and dissolute life, on afterwards repenting, to overcome in the time after repentance the evil conduct of a long time.
opinions.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians today agree in principle; the split appears over trust and office (should a repentant abuser or embezzler be restored to leadership?). Among the Fathers it was hotly contested (Tertullian, Novatian against).

opinions.position: Greek philosophy was God's gift to prepare the Greeks for Christ, as the Law prepared the Jews. Christians should use it, not fear it.
opinions.side_note: Pro-learning, including pagan philosophy (opposite Tertullian).
opinions.quote: Perchance, too, philosophy was given to the Greeks directly and primarily, till the Lord should call the Greeks. For this was a schoolmaster to bring the Hellenic mind, as the law, the Hebrews, to Christ.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many Christians today value secular study and see truth wherever it is found; a sizeable minority distrust secular philosophy and universities. Among the Fathers this is the classic Clement-versus-Tertullian clash.

opinions.position: Faith should be examined and grown with study. People who want "bare faith alone" are like farmers who want grapes without tending the vine.
opinions.side_note: For questioning and study, against unthinking faith.
opinions.quote: They demand bare faith alone, as if they wished, without bestowing any care on the vine, straightway to gather clusters from the first.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many believers prize simple trust and are wary of too much questioning; others think faith must be tested. Note Clement is not against faith: he means faith should grow into understanding.

opinions.position: God's good gifts may be enjoyed with gratitude; beauty is meant to lead us to praise its Maker. But luxury must be cut back hard.
opinions.side_note: Moderate enjoyment with thanksgiving; against luxury rather than against pleasure as such.
opinions.quote: As beauty, so also the flower delights when looked at; and it is meet to glorify the Creator by the enjoyment of the sight of beautiful objects.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today agree beauty may be enjoyed. The same chapter still forbids wearing flower crowns, so the balance is stricter than it sounds.

opinions.position: A pleasant word is fine, but clowning is not. Keep laughter in check: a smile suits a wise man; a guffaw is savage.
opinions.side_note: Restrained humour; against jokers and loud laughter.
opinions.quote: Pleasantry is allowable, not waggery. Besides, even laughter must be kept in check; for when given vent to in the right manner it indicates orderliness, but when it issues differently it shows a want of restraint.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today would disagree and love a good laugh; a minority value gravity. That makes it a sharp personality marker for a quiz.

opinions.position: The young should keep away from wine. Adults may take a little in the evening after serious reading is done, and the old may drink more cheerfully to warm their age, but never to the point of losing their reason.
opinions.side_note: Moderate drinking for adults, abstinence for the young.
opinions.quote: But towards evening, about supper-time, wine may be used, when we are no longer engaged in more serious readings.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many Christians drink moderately; Baptist, Methodist-heritage and Pentecostal traditions often abstain; Muslims and many health-minded people abstain. His "boys and girls" should keep "as much as possible away" from wine (same chapter).

opinions.position: The mature Christian thinks and speaks the truth, yet may sometimes tell an untruth for someone's good, as a doctor does for a patient. He never lies to deceive or harm.
opinions.side_note: A healing untruth can be allowed (against the strict no-lie view of Lactantius and Augustine).
opinions.quote: For he both thinks and speaks the truth; unless at any time, medicinally, as a physician for the safety of the sick, he may deceive or tell an untruth, according to the Sophists.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today accept some kind or protective lies; strict Christians (following Augustine and Kant) say never lie. The same chapter also says he is "never willing to lie by uttered word", so Clement's line is a narrow exception, not a licence.

opinions.position: Jesus told us to flee persecution. Someone who hands himself in, or provokes the authorities, shares the guilt of his own killing.
opinions.side_note: For flight; against volunteering for martyrdom.
opinions.quote: If he who kills a man of God sins against God, he also who presents himself before the judgment-seat becomes guilty of his death. And such is also the case with him who does not avoid persecution, but out of daring presents himself for capture.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians today agree one may flee danger. Among the Fathers it was contested: Tertullian in his Montanist years called flight a denial. Useful mainly as a contrast with Tertullian.

opinions.position: Staying single does not prove a man's worth. The married man who keeps his love for God through wife, children, servants and property proves more than the man who avoids them.
opinions.side_note: Marriage can be the harder and higher path (unusual among the Fathers, most of whom rank virginity higher).
opinions.quote: one is not really shown to be a man in the choice of single life; but he surpasses men, who, disciplined by marriage, procreation of children, and care for the house, without pleasure or pain, in his solicitude for the house has been inseparable from God's love
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Protestants and many people today would agree that family life is a school of holiness; Catholic and Orthodox tradition has ranked consecrated celibacy higher. Among the Fathers Clement is the rare voice for marriage, so it separates him sharply from Jerome.

opinions.position: The perfect Christian simply does not get angry, because he loves God and so hates none of God's creatures.
opinions.side_note: Against anger altogether (passionlessness); opposite of Lactantius, who says anger has a right use.
opinions.quote: Nor is he angry; for there is nothing to move him to anger, seeing he ever loves God, and is entirely turned towards Him alone, and therefore hates none of God's creatures.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today think some anger is healthy and right, especially at injustice; Buddhists, Stoic revivalists and some contemplatives would side with Clement. A clean split.

opinions.position: The mature Christian rises above feelings, even good ones such as courage and joy: nothing frightens him and nothing grieves him, because he trusts that all things happen well.
opinions.side_note: Feelings to be transcended (Stoic-leaning); opposite of Lactantius.
opinions.quote: Nor does he need cheerfulness of mind; for he does not fall into pain, being persuaded that all things happen well.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today, and most Christians, would reject this and say emotions are part of being human (Jesus wept). A minority drawn to Stoicism or detachment would like it. Strong contrast item.

opinions.position: Those who died without hearing the gospel are not simply lost. Christ and the apostles preached to the dead in Hades, and any who believe there, Gentiles included, are saved.
opinions.side_note: Hopeful for the unevangelized: a chance after death.
opinions.quote: If, accordingly, to all, then all who believe shall be saved, although they may be of the Gentiles, on making their profession there; since God's punishments are saving and disciplinary, leading to conversion
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many Christians today hope God will judge the unevangelized mercifully; conservative evangelicals often hold that explicit faith in this life is required; the idea of a post-mortem chance is a minority view.

opinions.position: God's punishments are meant to heal and correct, not only to pay back. He saves those who turn to Him. Clement leans hopeful but never states that all will be saved.
opinions.side_note: Punishment as correction; hopeful, stops short of universalism.
opinions.quote: If, then, in the deluge all sinful flesh perished, punishment having been inflicted on them for correction, we must first believe that the will of God, which is disciplinary and beneficent, saves those who turn to Him.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split today between those who see hell as corrective or final. Use Origen, not Clement, for the clear universalist pole.

opinions.position: A soldier who comes to faith need not leave the army; he should obey the commander who orders what is right.
opinions.side_note: Christians may stay soldiers (against Tertullian and Lactantius). Elsewhere he calls Christians "the bloodless host of peace" (Exhortation 11).
opinions.quote: Has knowledge taken hold of you while engaged in military service? Listen to the commander, who orders what is right.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians today accept military service; pacifist churches (Mennonite, Quaker, Brethren) do not. "Commander" may also be read as God. Useful only as a mild contrast.

opinions.position: Christians should stay away from the theatre and the racecourse: they breed lust, riots and waste, and a wise city does not make a business of its pastimes.
opinions.side_note: Against public entertainment of the time.
opinions.quote: Let spectacles, therefore, and plays that are full of scurrility and of abundant gossip, be forbidden.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Nearly one-sided among the Fathers. Today most people see no problem with plays or sport; a minority avoid crude or violent entertainment. Reframe for a quiz (for example, about shows full of crude talk).

opinions.position: No pipes, flutes, drums or cymbals at Christian feasts: they belong to shepherds, war and idol worship. Singing to the lyre or harp is fine.
opinions.side_note: Selective about instruments; for simple sung praise.
opinions.quote: And even if you wish to sing and play to the harp or lyre, there is no blame.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Today almost nobody objects to flutes; the live split is instruments in worship at all (Churches of Christ, Orthodox and some Reformed sing unaccompanied). The same chapter says "Let the pipe be resigned to the shepherds".

opinions.position: Aim for the middle: neither luxury nor stinginess, neither idleness nor exhaustion.
opinions.side_note: The moderate middle way, not extreme self-denial.
opinions.quote: Our mode of life is not to accustom us to voluptuousness and licentiousness, nor to the opposite extreme, but to the medium between these, that which is harmonious and temperate, and free of either evil, luxury and parsimony.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree with moderation in principle, so the statement alone tells a quiz little; it works as the moderate pole against the desert ascetics.

opinions.position: Exercise is good for body and courage: let men wrestle, play ball in the sun, walk, even use a hoe. But not for vanity, and never so much it wears you out.
opinions.side_note: Pro exercise and games, for health not glory. He keeps women to housework as exercise.
opinions.quote: In the case of men, let some strip and engage in wrestling; let some play at the small ball, especially the game they call Pheninda, in the sun.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost everyone today agrees exercise is good, so the plain claim is one-sided; his gender rules would be rejected by most. Use for colour in the portrait, not as a statement.

opinions.topic: new: make-up, hair dye and looks
opinions.position: Cosmetics, hair dye and shaving the body are signs of a sick soul. True beauty is inside.
opinions.side_note: Against cosmetics and grooming for show.
opinions.quote: Just as the plastered hand and the anointed eye exhibit from their very look the suspicion of a person in illness, so also cosmetics and dyes indicate that the soul is deeply diseased.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today reject this; some conservative churches (Holiness, Apostolic Pentecostal, some Anabaptist groups) still discourage make-up. A statement like "How you look says a lot about your soul" would split people.

opinions.topic: new: breaking with the customs you were raised in
opinions.position: Custom is not a reason. If your family's ways are wrong, leave them, as you left your baby food.
opinions.side_note: Truth over inherited custom.
opinions.quote: thus custom pleases and tickles; but custom pushes into the abyss, while truth conducts to heaven.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Traditionalists (religious and cultural) value inherited ways; many modern people prize breaking with the past. Note the target was pagan worship, not Christian tradition.

opinions.topic: new: being the same person in church and out
opinions.position: Many people are pious in church and then change colour like an octopus on a rock the moment they leave. Be, not seem.
opinions.side_note: Against church-only piety.
opinions.quote: Such ought those who are consecrated to Christ appear, and frame themselves in their whole life, as they fashion themselves in the church for the sake of gravity; and to be, not to seem such — so meek, so pious, so loving.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost everyone agrees in principle, so as a claim it is one-sided; useful as a vivid line in his portrait.

opinions.topic: new: are men and women capable of the same virtue?
opinions.position: Women and men, slave and free, share one nature and so one virtue. He still assigns child-bearing and housekeeping to women.
opinions.side_note: Same virtue and calling to holiness for both sexes.
opinions.quote: Accordingly woman is to practice self-restraint and righteousness, and every other virtue, as well as man, both bond and free; since it is a fit consequence that the same nature possesses one and the same virtue.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Nearly everyone today agrees; a live split would be on distinct roles, which he also holds. Portrait colour rather than a statement.

opinions.position: Prayer needs no words or special hours. The mature Christian prays silently, in every place, while walking, talking and reading.
opinions.side_note: For silent, continual prayer over set times and places.
opinions.quote: Prayer, then, may be uttered without the voice, by concentrating the whole spiritual nature within on expression by the mind, in un-distracted turning towards God.
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split between people who pray best in set words and times (liturgical, Muslim-style set prayer) and those who pray silently and continuously. Good for a temperament quiz.

opinions.position: Sleep on a firm bed, eat lightly, and rise at night to read or work. Too much sleep is a little death.
opinions.side_note: Against soft beds and long sleep.
opinions.quote: For those who have the sleepless Word dwelling in them, ought not to sleep the livelong night; but they ought to rise by night, especially when the days are coming to an end, and one devote himself to literature, another begin his art, the women handle the distaff, and all of us should, so to speak, fight against sleep
opinions.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today would disagree (sleep science praises long sleep); early risers and night-prayer traditions would agree. Fun personality item.

sparring.over: Whether martyrs suffer as punishment for hidden sins; also marriage and continence
Epiphanes taught common ownership of wives; Clement attacks his book On Justice
Tatian condemned marriage as corruption; Clement defends marriage as holy
He says those who hand themselves over "banish themselves without being martyrs"
Whether Greek learning is dangerous; he says they fear it "as children are at masks"

sparring.over: Lists his works among books not received by the Church
sparring.source: Decretum Gelasianum, list of works not received (English tr. Roger Pearse)
