figures.name: Origen
also_known_as: Adamantius ("man of steel"; Jerome: "man of adamant")
figures.places: Born and taught at Alexandria, Egypt; later settled at Caesarea in Palestine; visited Rome, Arabia, Antioch, Athens and Cappadocia; died at Tyre, where he was buried (Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 54).
figures.role: Teacher, biblical scholar (the Hexapla), preacher and commentator; head of the Alexandrian catechetical school at eighteen; presbyter at Caesarea; the most prolific Christian writer of his age.
figures.status_note: Never venerated as a saint. Admired by Pamphilus the martyr and Eusebius, who wrote a Defense of him, and used by the Cappadocians; attacked from the 390s by Epiphanius, Theophilus of Alexandria and Jerome. The Gelasian Decree receives only the works "which the blessed man Jerome does not reject". Emperor Justinian condemned Origenist teachings, and the Fifth Ecumenical Council (Constantinople, 553) names Origen among heretics in its eleventh anathema. What was condemned: the pre-existence of souls, a restoration of all things including demons, and related speculations. Cautions: much of his work survives only in Rufinus's Latin, which Rufinus admitted smoothing, or in hostile quotations by Jerome; the self-castration story rests on Eusebius alone and some modern scholars doubt it; he explicitly rejected reincarnation and denied teaching that the devil would be saved. He was tortured in the Decian persecution and died a few years later, so many count him a confessor.
figures.hook: As a teenager he was so set on dying with his arrested father that his mother hid all his clothes to keep him home.

stories.story: When his father Leonides was arrested, the boy Origen rushed to join him in martyrdom. His mother begged him, then hid all his clothes so he had to stay home. He wrote to his father instead: "Take heed not to change your mind on our account."

As a child he pestered his father with questions about the hidden meaning of Scripture. Leonides scolded him to his face, but would stand over the sleeping boy, uncover his chest "as if the Divine Spirit were enshrined within it", and kiss it.
To teach the faith for free he sold his library of classical books for four obols a day, slept on the floor, went barefoot for years, fasted and gave up wine, until friends feared for his health.
During persecution he openly kissed condemned martyrs on the way to execution; crowds nearly lynched him, and soldiers surrounded the house where he taught, so he moved from house to house.

Reading "eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven" literally, and teaching women as well as men, he castrated himself. Eusebius calls it the act of "an immature and youthful mind"; his bishop Demetrius first praised it, then used it against him when Origen grew famous.
For his six-column Bible (the Hexapla) he learned Hebrew and hunted lost Greek translations, one of which he says he found "in a jar in Jericho".

In the Decian persecution he endured the iron collar, the dungeon, and days with his feet stretched "four spaces in the stocks", while the judge tried hard to keep him alive so he could not die a martyr. He died a few years later.

temperament.evidence: He dictated to "more than seven amanuenses, who relieved each other at appointed times", with copyists and girls skilled in fine writing, all paid for by his patron Ambrose.
"His manner of life was as his doctrine, and his doctrine as his life."

His pupil Gregory says love for him was kindled "like some spark lighting upon our inmost soul"; he refuted pupils "in the genuine Socratic fashion" until they were quiet "like so many unbroken steeds" brought to the bridle.
temperament.source: Gregory Thaumaturgus, Oration and Panegyric addressed to Origen 6-7

temperament.evidence: Excommunicated by Demetrius, he wrote that he would not even speak evil of the devil, and that "we ought to pity them, not to hate them".
temperament.source: His letter to friends in Alexandria, quoted by Jerome, Apology against Rufinus 2.18

temperament.evidence: Eusebius shows him running toward martyrdom as a boy, living at the "very extreme of poverty", and taking Scripture so literally that he mutilated himself.

genuine_lines.quote: Take heed not to change your mind on our account.
genuine_lines.work: Letter to his father Leonides in prison (lost), quoted by Eusebius
genuine_lines.translation: A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 1 (1890), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: We ought to pity them, not to hate them, to pray for them, not to curse them. For we have been created for blessing, not for cursing.
genuine_lines.work: Letter to friends in Alexandria (lost in Greek), quoted by Jerome
genuine_lines.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 3 (1892), as revised for New Advent (Jerome's Latin rendering of Origen's Greek)

genuine_lines.quote: For stronger than all the evils in the soul is the Word, and the healing power that dwells in Him; and this healing He applies, according to the will of God, to every man.
genuine_lines.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For we who read the things of God need much application, lest we should say or think anything too rashly about them.
genuine_lines.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: The individual ought, then, to portray the ideas of holy Scripture in a threefold manner upon his own soul; in order that the simple man may be edified by the flesh, as it were, of the Scripture, for so we name the obvious sense
genuine_lines.location: Book 4, chapter 1, section 11 (translated from the Greek of the Philocalia)
genuine_lines.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: It is not irrational, then, to form associations in opposition to existing laws, if done for the sake of the truth.
genuine_lines.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent

misattributed.line: "Origen taught reincarnation" (common in New Age and some popular writing, often with the claim that a council removed reincarnation from the Bible).
misattributed.truth: He rejected transmigration by name: "the dogma of transmigration, which is foreign to the church of God" (Commentary on Matthew 13.1, ANF vol. 9). He did teach that souls existed before birth, a different idea that was later condemned. No council removed anything about reincarnation from the Bible.

misattributed.line: "Origen said even the devil will be saved."
misattributed.truth: His opponents drew this from his system, and the Valentinian Candidus claimed he said it; Origen denied it in a letter as "a thing which not even a madman can say" (quoted by Jerome, Apology against Rufinus 2.18). His Latin works do speak of the final subjection of all enemies, so the question stayed disputed.

misattributed.line: The "Penitence of Origen", a lament presented as his own confession.
misattributed.truth: A later text falsely attributed to him (see "Pseudo-Origen" and "Penitence of Origen" in standard references); not by Origen.

misattributed.line: Quotations from On First Principles presented as Origen's exact words.
misattributed.truth: Most of that work survives only in Rufinus's free Latin version, which he openly edited to remove what he thought heretical interpolations; Jerome's more literal fragments sometimes differ. Treat Latin-only passages as Origen as filtered by Rufinus.

opinions.position: Take from Greek philosophy and science whatever serves Christ, as Israel took gold from Egypt to build the tabernacle.
opinions.side_note: Pro-learning; "spoiling the Egyptians".
opinions.quote: I wish to ask you to extract from the philosophy of the Greeks what may serve as a course of study or a preparation for Christianity, and from geometry and astronomy what will serve to explain the sacred Scriptures
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most educated Christians today agree; a minority distrust secular learning. Among the Fathers, Origen and Clement are the pole opposite Tertullian.

opinions.topic: new: reading books you disagree with
opinions.position: Students should read every philosopher and poet, holding nothing back, except outright atheists; nothing is a forbidden subject.
opinions.side_note: Read widely, including opponents. Recorded by his pupil, not in his own words.
opinions.quote: For he deemed it right for us to study philosophy in such wise, that we should read with utmost diligence all that has been written, both by the philosophers and by the poets of old, rejecting nothing, and repudiating nothing
opinions.work: Gregory Thaumaturgus, Oration and Panegyric addressed to Origen (a pupil's eyewitness account)
opinions.location: argument before section 13 (New Advent numbering: section 13)
opinions.translation: S. D. F. Salmond, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 6 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many people today say read your opponents; many religious parents and some churches limit what young believers read. Strong quiz candidate: "I read books by people I think are wrong."

opinions.position: The apostles taught the essentials plainly but left the reasons and many deep questions open, on purpose, so that lovers of wisdom would search them out.
opinions.side_note: For open inquiry within the rule of faith.
opinions.quote: while on other subjects they merely stated the fact that things were so, keeping silence as to the manner or origin of their existence; clearly in order that the more zealous of their successors, who should be lovers of wisdom, might have a subject of exercise on which to display the fruit of their talents
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), from Rufinus's Latin version, as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split between those who love theological speculation and those who think we should not go beyond what is plainly revealed. Good statement.

opinions.position: Ideally everyone would examine the reasons for their faith. But most people have neither time nor ability, so simple faith that changes a life is a real good, not a second-class faith.
opinions.side_note: Examined faith is best; simple faith is good for the many.
opinions.quote: To which we have to answer, that if it were possible for all to leave the business of life, and devote themselves to philosophy, no other method ought to be adopted by any one, but this alone.
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Intellectual believers and sceptics value examined belief; many believers value childlike trust. His two-tier view (thinkers and simple believers) itself divides people.

opinions.position: Some Bible passages cannot be literally true, and are there to push readers to a deeper, spiritual meaning. Who could think there were days and evenings before the sun existed?
opinions.side_note: Allegorical and spiritual reading over strict literalism.
opinions.quote: For who that has understanding will suppose that the first, and second, and third day, and the evening and the morning, existed without a sun, and moon, and stars?
opinions.location: Book 4, chapter 1, section 16 (translated from the Greek of the Philocalia)
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Sharply split. Young-earth and literalist Christians reject this; most mainline, Catholic and Orthodox readers and non-believers accept non-literal readings of Genesis. One of the best statements available. Note: the New Advent page contains invisible soft hyphens inside some words of this sentence (sup-pose, ex-isted).

opinions.position: In the end the Word of God will win over every rational being and heal every soul; no evil in the soul is too strong for Him. He left open whether evil could ever arise again.
opinions.side_note: The classic hopeful-universalist pole.
opinions.quote: But our belief is, that the Word shall prevail over the entire rational creation, and change every soul into His own perfection
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Most traditional Christians hold that some are finally lost; a growing minority (and many non-Christians) hope all will be saved. Origen is the flagship for the hopeful pole. His later condemnation (553) should be noted in any reveal.

opinions.topic: new: will the devil be saved?
opinions.position: He denied, angrily, that he ever taught that the devil would be saved; people who claimed so misrepresented him.
opinions.side_note: No salvation for the devil, by his own letter; disputed because of his wider system.
opinions.quote: namely, that the father of wickedness and perdition of those who shall be cast out of the kingdom of God can be saved; a thing which not even a madman can say.
opinions.work: Letter to friends in Alexandria (lost in Greek), quoted by Jerome
opinions.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 3 (1892), as revised for New Advent (Jerome's Latin rendering of Origen's Greek)
opinions.today: Nearly everyone today, Christian or not, would say the devil (if he exists) is not saved; a tiny minority of universalists would disagree. Mainly useful to correct a popular myth about Origen.

opinions.position: Hell's fire is not a furnace waiting outside us. Each sinner lights his own fire; his sins are the fuel, and his conscience, seeing all he did, is the torment.
opinions.side_note: Hell as inner, self-made torment of conscience.
opinions.quote: By these words it seems to be indicated that every sinner kindles for himself the flame of his own fire, and is not plunged into some fire which has been already kindled by another, or was in existence before himself. Of this fire the fuel and food are our sins
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), from Rufinus's Latin version, as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many modern Christians and C. S. Lewis readers find hell-as-self-chosen persuasive; others hold a literal place of fire. Clear, relatable statement.

opinions.position: Christians do not fight in the emperor's wars even when ordered. They serve him better by prayer, like priests whose hands stay free of blood, and they pray for those fighting in a righteous cause.
opinions.side_note: Christians should not bear arms, though war itself may be just for others.
opinions.quote: We do not indeed fight under him, although he require it; but we fight on his behalf, forming a special army — an army of piety— by offering our prayers to God.
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians today accept military service; pacifist churches side with Origen. Good split statement: "A Christian should refuse to fight even if the country calls."

opinions.position: Christians decline public office, not to dodge duty, but to serve in the Church for the salvation of people.
opinions.side_note: Against Christians taking political office.
opinions.quote: And it is not for the purpose of escaping public duties that Christians decline public offices, but that they may reserve themselves for a diviner and more necessary service in the Church of God— for the salvation of men.
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians today think believers should serve in government; Anabaptist and some separatist groups agree with Origen. Clear split.

opinions.topic: new: choosing leaders who do not want the job
opinions.position: The Church should reject people who are ambitious to lead and press the modest, who hang back, to take charge.
opinions.side_note: Prefer reluctant leaders.
opinions.quote: Those who are ambitious of ruling we reject; but we constrain those who, through excess of modesty, are not easily induced to take a public charge in the Church of God.
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many people say "never trust someone who wants power"; others think ambition and drive make good leaders. Strong, everyday statement.

opinions.position: When a state's laws are ungodly, it is right to meet and organise against them for the sake of truth, as people would rightly conspire against a tyrant.
opinions.side_note: For civil disobedience against unjust laws.
opinions.quote: It is not irrational, then, to form associations in opposition to existing laws, if done for the sake of the truth. For as those persons would do well who should enter into a secret association in order to put to death a tyrant who had seized upon the liberties of a state
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many admire civil disobedience (King, Bonhoeffer); others stress obeying the authorities (Romans 13). Note his tyrant example is an analogy; the Christian "league" he means is against the devil and idolatry, not armed revolt.

opinions.position: Christians who fall into grave sin are mourned as dead, but if they truly change they are received back after a longer wait. They are never again given office in the Church.
opinions.side_note: Restore the fallen, but not to leadership.
opinions.quote: and as being risen from the dead (if they manifest a becoming change) they receive them afterwards, at some future time, after a greater interval than in the case of those who were admitted at first, but not placing in any office or post of rank in the Church of God those who, after professing the Gospel, lapsed and fell.
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Very live today: should a fallen pastor ever lead again? Many say forgive but never restore to leadership; others say full restoration is grace. Excellent quiz material.

opinions.position: Miracles did not stop with the apostles. In his own day Christians still drove out evil spirits, healed and foresaw events.
opinions.side_note: Signs continue.
opinions.quote: And there are still preserved among Christians traces of that Holy Spirit which appeared in the form of a dove. They expel evil spirits, and perform many cures, and foresee certain events, according to the will of the Logos.
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split today between Pentecostals and charismatics (signs continue) and cessationists and sceptics. Among the Fathers nearly everyone claimed ongoing miracles, so it is one-sided there.

opinions.position: God never lies. A person, when necessity forces it, may use a falsehood for a great good, carefully and sparingly, like a medicine, as Judith, Esther and Jacob did.
opinions.side_note: A necessary lie can be allowed (known only through Jerome's hostile quotation of his lost Stromata).
opinions.quote: But a man on whom necessity imposes the responsibility of lying is bound to use very great care, and to use falsehood as he would a stimulant or a medicine, and strictly to preserve its measure
opinions.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 3 (1892), as revised for New Advent (Jerome's Latin rendering of Origen's Greek)
opinions.today: Most people today accept a lie in real necessity (hiding refugees); strict Christians following Augustine say never. Pairs perfectly against Lactantius.

opinions.position: When Scripture speaks of God's wrath it does not mean He feels a passion. "Wrath" is a way of speaking about His stern discipline of sinners.
opinions.side_note: God's anger is figurative (opposite of Lactantius, who says God truly is angry).
opinions.quote: We do not, however, assert that it indicates any passion on His part, but that it is something which is assumed in order to discipline by stern means those sinners who have committed many and grievous sins.
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many believers today affirm a God who is truly angry at evil; others think talk of divine anger is metaphor. Good theological pair with Lactantius.

opinions.position: Our growth takes real effort on our part, like a farmer's work, yet the harvest is God's doing and the credit is His.
opinions.side_note: Effort and grace together; free will stressed against fatalism.
opinions.quote: so also is our own perfection brought about, not indeed by our remaining inactive and idle, (but by some activity on our part): and yet the consummation of it will not be ascribed to us, but to God, who is the first and chief cause of the work.
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), from Rufinus's Latin version, as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians would sign this middle position; the split comes when pushed toward "it is all grace" or "it is up to me". Useful as the synergy pole.

opinions.topic: new: why are people born unequal?
opinions.position: God made all souls equal. The differences between beings, and the circumstances they are born into, come from their own free choices before birth, not from God's favouritism.
opinions.side_note: Pre-existence of souls; later condemned.
opinions.quote: this freedom of will incited each one either to progress by imitation of God, or reduced him to failure through negligence. And this, as we have already stated, is the cause of the diversity among rational creatures, deriving its origin not from the will or judgment of the Creator, but from the freedom of the individual will.
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), from Rufinus's Latin version, as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians today reject pre-existence of souls; the question behind it (is life's unfairness God's choice?) still splits people. Handle with care: this is one of the condemned teachings.

opinions.position: Souls do not return in new bodies; transmigration is foreign to the Church and to Scripture.
opinions.side_note: Against reincarnation (despite popular claims).
opinions.quote: lest I should fall into the dogma of transmigration, which is foreign to the church of God, and not handed down by the Apostles, nor anywhere set forth in the Scriptures
opinions.translation: John Patrick, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 9 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split in the wider public: about a quarter to a third of Americans say they believe in reincarnation (Pew surveys), while Christian teaching rejects it. Among the Fathers it is one-sided.

opinions.position: Christians do not build lifeless temples and statues to God. Their bodies and souls are the temple, and the virtues are the images.
opinions.side_note: Against temple and image worship in his day.
opinions.quote: we do not object to the erection of temples suited to the images and altars of which we have spoken, but that we do refuse to build lifeless temples to the Giver of all life
opinions.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split today between those who value beautiful churches and icons and those who say the building does not matter. Note: he is answering pagan charges before Christians built great churches.

opinions.position: Even when bishops condemned him unfairly, he would not curse them: pity and pray for opponents; we were made to bless.
opinions.side_note: Bless, do not curse, your opponents.
opinions.quote: We ought to pity them, not to hate them, to pray for them, not to curse them.
opinions.work: Letter to friends in Alexandria (lost in Greek), quoted by Jerome
opinions.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 3 (1892), as revised for New Advent (Jerome's Latin rendering of Origen's Greek)
opinions.today: Everyone agrees in principle; the real split is whether to call out opponents publicly and sharply (as Jerome did). Pair with Jerome for a clean contrast.

opinions.position: As a boy he urged his imprisoned father not to deny Christ for the family's sake, though it meant losing him and everything they owned.
opinions.side_note: Faithfulness over family safety.
opinions.quote: Take heed not to change your mind on our account.
opinions.work: Letter to his father (lost), quoted by Eusebius
opinions.translation: A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 1 (1890), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many would say a father should protect his family first; others honour standing firm whatever the cost. Powerful and personal.

sparring.over: Origen's ordination as presbyter in Palestine and his preaching as a layman before bishops; Demetrius "wrote everywhere to injure his reputation" and had him condemned
sparring.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.8, 6.19.16-19, 6.23; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 54

sparring.over: Whether the story of Susanna is genuine Scripture; a courteous exchange of letters, Origen defending the Greek Daniel used by the churches
sparring.source: Africanus, Letter to Origen; Origen, Letter to Africanus

sparring.over: Whether Christ existed as a distinct person before the incarnation; Origen argued him round at a synod
In a public debate Candidus said Origen taught the devil could be saved; Origen denied it and complained the record was falsified
The resurrection body and free will; Methodius wrote "On the resurrection, against Origen"
sparring.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 83; Methodius, Discourse on the Resurrection

sparring.over: Once his great admirer ("our Christian man of brass, or, rather, man of adamant"), Jerome later insisted "I have praised the commentator but not the theologian"

sparring.with: Epiphanius of Salamis and Theophilus of Alexandria (after his death)
sparring.over: Led the campaign against Origenists around 400; imperial rescripts banished Origenists from Alexandria and Egypt
sparring.source: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus 1.12 (mentions the letters of Theophilus and Epiphanius, which Jerome translated, and the imperial rescripts)

sparring.over: Celsus's attack on Christianity, answered in eight books; Porphyry, who had met him, mocked his allegorical reading

portraits.title: Origen (portrait used on Wikipedia)
portraits.kind: portrait (imagined likeness; details of the original not recorded on the file page)

portraits.title: Origen in the Nuremberg Chronicle
portraits.artist: Hartmann Schedel (chronicle); workshop of Michael Wolgemut and Wilhelm Pleydenwurff

portraits.title: Origen (medieval miniature from a Roman de la Rose manuscript, MS. Douce 195)
portraits.kind: manuscript illumination (colour); shows the self-castration, so unsuitable for a result card

figures.name: Lactantius
figures.places: North Africa (his youth; Jerome says he wrote his Banquet "as a young man in Africa"); Nicomedia in Bithynia (modern Izmit, Turkey), where Diocletian summoned him to teach Latin rhetoric; Gaul, where in old age he tutored Constantine's son Crispus.
figures.role: Professor of Latin rhetoric and convert; pupil of Arnobius; the first Christian to set out the faith as a whole system in polished Latin (the Divine Institutes); eyewitness historian of the Great Persecution.
figures.status_note: Not a saint in any church and never venerated. The sixth-century Gelasian Decree lists "the works of Lactantius also known as Firmianus" among books not received. Jerome praised his style but faulted his teaching, and said he denied that the Holy Spirit is a distinct person. Cautions: he expected the world to end within two hundred years of his writing, after six thousand years of history, followed by a literal thousand-year reign of the saints on earth; he mocked the idea of a round earth with people on the other side; he writes with open relish about the painful deaths of persecutors. The addresses to Constantine in the Divine Institutes are missing from some manuscripts (ANF note).
figures.hook: A Latin professor in the emperor's city who watched soldiers tear down the church across from the palace, he wrote that a Christian may never kill anyone, not even in war or by bringing a death-penalty charge, and ended his days tutoring the emperor's son.

stories.story: Diocletian summoned him from Africa to teach Latin rhetoric at Nicomedia, the eastern capital. In a Greek-speaking city he had few pupils, so he turned to writing.

He describes the dawn in 303 when officials forced the doors of the church at Nicomedia, burned the Scriptures, and Diocletian and Galerius watched from the palace "as if on a watchtower", arguing whether to set it alight. The Praetorian Guard "in a few hours levelled that very lofty edifice with the ground."
stories.source: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 12

stories.story: While he was teaching in Bithynia and the church lay in ruins, two men mocked the Christians: one a philosopher who preached simple living but lived in luxury, the other a judge who wrote books against Christ. Their attacks moved him to write his defence of the faith.
He saw the governor of Bithynia "wonderfully elated with joy, as though he had subdued some nation of barbarians" because one Christian, after resisting for two years, finally seemed to give way.

He lived so poor that he "generally lacked even the necessities", yet in extreme old age he was chosen as tutor to Crispus, the son of Constantine, in Gaul. Crispus was later put to death by his own father.
stories.source: Jerome, Chronicle for the year 317 (tr. Roger Pearse); Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 80

stories.story: He is the earliest source for Constantine's dream before the battle at the Milvian Bridge (312): Constantine was told to mark "the heavenly sign" on his soldiers' shields, the cipher of Christ.
stories.source: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 44

stories.story: He describes in grisly detail how the persecutor Galerius died: his bowels rotted, worms swarmed from his body, and the stench "pervade[d] not only the palace, but even the whole city".
stories.source: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 33

temperament.evidence: He wished for eloquence "in some degree approaching" Cicero's, yet argued that "simple and undisguised truth" needs no ornament and that God made Scripture plain "that all might understand".
On people who believe in the antipodes: "is there any one so senseless as to believe that there are men whose footsteps are higher than their heads?"

temperament.trait: Openly glad at God's judgement on persecutors
temperament.evidence: He wrote a whole book so that later readers "may learn how the Almighty manifested His power ... in rooting out and utterly destroying the enemies of His name."
temperament.source: On the Deaths of the Persecutors 1

temperament.evidence: Tertullian "had little readiness, and was not sufficiently polished, and very obscure"; Cyprian should have argued with a pagan "by arguments and reason", not by quoting Scripture he rejected.

temperament.trait: Eloquent, by the verdict of a harsh critic
temperament.evidence: Jerome: "Lactantius has a flow of eloquence worthy of Tully".

genuine_lines.quote: For religion is to be defended, not by putting to death, but by dying; not by cruelty, but by patient endurance; not by guilt, but by good faith
genuine_lines.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For nothing is so much a matter of free-will as religion; in which, if the mind of the worshipper is disinclined to it, religion is at once taken away, and ceases to exist.
genuine_lines.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Therefore, with regard to this precept of God, there ought to be no exception at all; but that it is always unlawful to put to death a man, whom God willed to be a sacred animal.
genuine_lines.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For if God is not angry with the impious and the unrighteous, it is clear that He does not love the pious and the righteous.
genuine_lines.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Or is there any one so senseless as to believe that there are men whose footsteps are higher than their heads?
genuine_lines.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Wherefore it is undoubted that there is no religion wherever there is an image.
genuine_lines.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent

misattributed.line: The "Epicurean paradox" ("Is God willing to prevent evil, but not able? ... Then why call him God?"), quoted everywhere as the words of Epicurus.
misattributed.truth: The argument survives only in Lactantius, On the Anger of God 13, who attributes it to Epicurus in order to answer it. No Epicurean text contains it, and scholars doubt Epicurus framed it this way. The punchy modern wording ("Then why call him God?") is a later paraphrase, not ancient. The ancient form is: "God, he says, either wishes to take away evils, and is unable; or He is able, and is unwilling..."

misattributed.line: "Early Christians believed the earth was flat", with Lactantius as the proof.
misattributed.truth: Lactantius did reject a round earth with antipodes (Divine Institutes 3.24), but he was an outlier. Many Christian writers accepted a spherical earth, and the idea that the Church taught a flat earth is largely a nineteenth-century myth. Copernicus himself singled out Lactantius as an example of childish talk about the earth's shape, in the preface to On the Revolutions (1543).

misattributed.line: Stories that credit Eusebius alone with Constantine's vision of the cross.
misattributed.truth: Lactantius wrote the earliest account (On the Deaths of the Persecutors 44), and it is a dream about marking a sign on shields; Eusebius's later Life of Constantine adds a vision of a cross in the sky.

opinions.position: A just man may not fight in war at all; his warfare is justice itself. God's command against killing allows no exceptions.
opinions.side_note: Pacifist: no military service. Yet he celebrated Constantine's victory won under the sign of Christ (On the Deaths of the Persecutors 44).
opinions.quote: Thus it will be neither lawful for a just man to engage in warfare, since his warfare is justice itself, nor to accuse any one of a capital charge
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians today accept military service and just war; pacifist churches and many peace activists side with Lactantius. Pairs well against Augustine and Ambrose.

opinions.position: A Christian may not even bring a charge that could end in execution. Killing by words in court is still killing.
opinions.side_note: Against capital punishment entirely.
opinions.quote: because it makes no difference whether you put a man to death by word, or rather by the sword, since it is the act of putting to death itself which is prohibited.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Sharply split today: roughly half of Americans support the death penalty; the Catholic Church now calls it inadmissible; many evangelicals support it. Excellent statement.

opinions.topic: new: when you cannot afford children
opinions.position: Exposing a newborn is as wicked as killing it. If you are too poor to raise children, it is better not to marry than to "mar the work of God".
opinions.side_note: Against infant exposure; abstain rather than abandon.
opinions.quote: It is therefore as wicked to expose as it is to kill.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Everyone today condemns abandoning babies, so the plain line is one-sided. The live split is his remedy: "If you are too poor to raise children, it is better to abstain from marriage" (same chapter).

opinions.position: Watching a man die for entertainment makes you a sharer in murder, even if he was justly condemned. All the shows should be avoided.
opinions.side_note: Against violent spectacle and the theatre.
opinions.quote: For he who reckons it a pleasure, that a man, though justly condemned, should be slain in his sight, pollutes his conscience as much as if he should become a spectator and a sharer of a homicide which is secretly committed.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Nearly one-sided among the Fathers. Today the live version is violent entertainment (combat sports, gory films, true-crime): people split on whether enjoying it harms you.

opinions.position: Pleasant sounds are easily ignored, but song and poetry capture the heart, so choose them carefully. If you love melody, sing the praises of God.
opinions.side_note: Sacred song over worldly song.
opinions.quote: Therefore, if it be a pleasure to hear melodies and songs, let it be pleasant to sing and hear the praises of God.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Some Christians listen only to worship music; most enjoy all kinds. Good personal statement.

opinions.position: Never lie, not even to an enemy or a stranger. Your tongue must always match your mind.
opinions.side_note: Strict: no lie ever (opposite of Clement and Origen).
opinions.quote: but he will think that it is not his part to speak falsely even to an enemy and a stranger; nor will he at any time so act, that his tongue, which is the interpreter of his mind, should be at variance with his feeling and thought.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today would lie to an enemy to protect someone; strict Christians and Kantians would not. The contrast with Origen's "falsehood as a medicine" is ideal for the quiz.

opinions.position: If you lend money, take no interest. Profiting from someone's need is lying in wait for booty.
opinions.side_note: Against interest on loans.
opinions.quote: If he shall have lent any money, he will not receive interest, that the benefit may be unimpaired which succours necessity, and that he may entirely abstain from the property of another.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Most people accept interest; Islamic finance forbids it, and many think lending to a friend in need should be interest-free. A personal version ("I would never charge a friend interest") splits well.

opinions.position: Returning an injury is as bad as starting one. Bear wrongs calmly and leave revenge to God.
opinions.side_note: No retaliation.
opinions.quote: For it is not less the part of a bad man to return an injury than to inflict it.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Sharply split. Many people today think standing up for yourself and hitting back is healthy; others hold to turning the other cheek. Strong statement.

opinions.position: God gave us anger for one purpose: to correct wrongdoing in those in our care, such as children. Using it against equals is wicked and dangerous.
opinions.side_note: Anger has a right use (against Clement's passionless ideal), but only for correcting the young.
opinions.quote: Therefore, as it is both just and necessary to employ anger towards the young, so it is both pernicious and impious to use it towards those of our own age.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most parents today reject angry discipline of children; many think anger at equals over injustice is healthy. So it splits in an unusual direction.

opinions.position: Feelings are planted in us by God. The Stoics are mad to try to cut them out; they should be directed to the right ends.
opinions.side_note: Emotions are good when rightly directed (opposite of Clement's passionlessness).
opinions.quote: The Stoics therefore are mad who do not regulate but cut them out, and wish by some means or other to deprive man of powers implanted in him by nature.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today agree feelings are part of being human; a minority prize detachment. Good pair with Clement.

opinions.position: God truly is angry at evil. A God who is never angry with the wicked cannot really love the good.
opinions.side_note: Real divine anger (opposite of Origen, who reads it as a figure of speech).
opinions.quote: Thus, he who loves the good also hates the wicked, and he who does not hate the wicked does not love the good
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many believers say God's wrath is real and part of His love; others find it hard to square with a loving God. Strong statement.

opinions.position: God could remove evil but does not, because without evil there would be no wisdom and no virtue; we could not know good without knowing evil.
opinions.side_note: Evil permitted for the sake of wisdom and virtue.
opinions.quote: For on this account He does not take them away, because He at the same time gives wisdom, as I have shown; and there is more of goodness and pleasure in wisdom than of annoyance in evils.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many believers accept a "soul-making" answer; sceptics and many sufferers find it inadequate. A statement like "Suffering is how we grow wise" divides people well.

opinions.position: Religion cannot be forced. It must be spread by words, not blows, because faith that is compelled is not faith at all.
opinions.side_note: For religious freedom; against coercion (opposite of the later Augustine).
opinions.quote: There is no occasion for violence and injury, for religion cannot be imposed by force; the matter must be carried on by words rather than by blows, that the will may be affected.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people in free countries agree; the split today is over how far the state should favour or protect a religion. Among the Fathers it is a real clash with Augustine's later support for coercing the Donatists.

opinions.position: Where there is an image, there is no true religion; religion is heavenly, and images are earthly.
opinions.side_note: Against images in worship (aimed at pagan idols).
opinions.quote: Wherefore it is undoubted that there is no religion wherever there is an image.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split today between Orthodox and Catholics (icons and statues) and Reformed Protestants and Muslims (none). Caution: his target is pagan idols; do not present it as a ruling on Christian icons.

opinions.position: Christians call each other brothers and sisters because they believe they are equal: rich and poor, slave and master. God distinguishes people only by virtue.
opinions.side_note: Equality before God, across class.
opinions.quote: There is none; nor is there any other cause why we mutually bestow upon each other the name of brethren, except that we believe ourselves to be equal.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost everyone agrees in principle today, so one-sided as a bare claim; useful as a line in his portrait.

opinions.position: Give to people who can never pay you back. Giving to the "suitable", who can return the favour, is really investing in yourself.
opinions.side_note: Generosity to those who cannot repay (against Cicero's advice).
opinions.quote: For we must not bestow our bounty on suitable objects, but as much as possible on unsuitable objects.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split in practice: many give to causes that benefit their own circles; others give where it cannot be returned. A good statement.

opinions.position: The last and greatest work of kindness is to bury strangers and the poor, doing for an unknown man what his family would do.
opinions.side_note: Care for the unclaimed dead.
opinions.quote: The last and greatest office of piety is the burying of strangers and the poor; which subject those teachers of virtue and justice have not touched upon at all.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost no one objects; it tells a quiz little as a claim but gives his portrait warmth.

opinions.position: Pagan philosophy is empty and false; true wisdom and true religion cannot be separated, and both come from God.
opinions.side_note: Suspicious of philosophy (closer to Tertullian than to Clement), though himself highly educated.
opinions.quote: it is the business of this book to show the emptiness and falsehood of philosophy also, that, all error being removed, the truth may be brought to light and become manifest.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Some believers see philosophy as a threat; others as an ally. He contrasts well with Clement and Origen.

opinions.position: If people are made for wisdom, then workers, farmers, women and slaves should all be taught it, not just the rich and leisured.
opinions.side_note: Education for all classes and both sexes.
opinions.quote: But if the nature of man is capable of wisdom, it was befitting that both workmen, and country people, and women, and all, in short, who bear the human form, should be taught to be wise
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Nearly everyone agrees today, so it works as portrait colour rather than a statement.

opinions.position: He ridiculed philosophers who said the earth is round and people live on the other side, calling it one error defended by another.
opinions.side_note: Against a spherical earth with antipodes (an outlier view even then).
opinions.quote: How is it with those who imagine that there are antipodes opposite to our footsteps? Do they say anything to the purpose?
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: On the earth's shape, virtually no one today agrees with him, so do not use it as a statement. The underlying temperament (trusting common sense over expert theory) does split people.

opinions.position: Husbands are bound by exactly the same law of faithfulness as wives. A married man who sleeps with a slave or any other woman is an adulterer before God.
opinions.side_note: One standard of faithfulness for both sexes; no divorce except for adultery.
opinions.quote: But as a woman is bound by the bonds of chastity not to desire any other man, so let the husband be bound by the same law, since God has joined together the husband and the wife in the union of one body.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost everyone agrees on the double standard today; the split is on divorce only for adultery. The full Divine Institutes 6.23 on this subject is left in Latin in the ANF.

opinions.position: Repentance always has a harbour. If we take back children we once disinherited when they repent, how much more will God our Father.
opinions.side_note: For second chances.
opinions.quote: For if we think that our children are corrected when we perceive that they repent of their faults, and though we have disinherited and cast them off, we again receive, cherish, and embrace them, why should we despair that the mercy of God our Father may again be appeased by repentance?
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree about God; the split comes over whether people should always take back those who wronged them.

opinions.position: History lasts six thousand years, then a thousand-year reign of the just on earth. By his reckoning the end was at most two hundred years away.
opinions.side_note: Literal millennium; near end of the world.
opinions.quote: And again, since God, having finished His works, rested the seventh day and blessed it, at the end of the six thousandth year all wickedness must be abolished from the earth, and righteousness reign for a thousand years
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many evangelicals expect a literal millennium and a near end; Catholics, Orthodox and most mainline Protestants do not. A general statement ("I expect the end of the world in my lifetime or soon after") would split people.

opinions.position: When you argue with someone who rejects the Bible, do not quote the Bible at him. Use reason and his own authorities.
opinions.side_note: Reason first with outsiders.
opinions.quote: for he ought to have been refuted not by the testimonies of Scripture, which he plainly considered vain, fictitious, and false, but by arguments and reason.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Evidentialist apologists agree; presuppositionalists and many preachers say Scripture speaks for itself. Clean statement.

opinions.topic: new: plain words over fine speech
opinions.position: God made Scripture plain on purpose, so everyone could understand it; the educated who despise it for its plain style are chasing the wrong pleasure.
opinions.side_note: Plain truth over eloquence.
opinions.quote: Yea, rather, with the greatest foresight, He wished those things which are divine to be without adornment, that all might understand the things which He Himself spoke to all.
opinions.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split in taste: some prefer plain modern Bibles and sermons, others value beautiful language and liturgy.

sparring.over: Praised his eloquence but wished "he had been as ready to teach our doctrines as he was to pull down those of others"; also said he denied that the Holy Spirit is a distinct person
Method: Cyprian answered the pagan Demetrianus with Scripture texts the man thought false; Lactantius says he should have used arguments and reason
Style: "not sufficiently polished, and very obscure", so his defence of the faith failed to win readers
Lists his works among books not received

sparring.with: Two anti-Christian writers at Nicomedia: a luxury-loving philosopher and a judge (usually identified as Sossianus Hierocles)
sparring.over: Their attacks on Christians during the persecution, which he answered in the Divine Institutes
